title: Gall's law and the test for whether complexity was earned

claims.text: John Gall, in Systemantics: How Systems Work and Especially How They Fail, published in 1975, states what is now known as Gall's law: a complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked; a complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched up to make it work, so one has to start over with a working simple system.

source.title: John Gall, Systemantics: How Systems Work and Especially How They Fail, Quadrangle/The New York Times Book Co., 1975

beats.broke: complexity is added for a future that is described rather than observed, and it is indistinguishable at the time from competence, because both look like thinking ahead
beats.fix: require a specific event as the justification for each piece of complexity, since a real constraint can be named and an imagined one can only be described
beats.cost: the test is conservative by construction and will refuse some complexity that turns out to be needed, at the price of paying for it later when the evidence exists
beats.interview: how to tell a design that anticipates from one that speculates
